summary: As leaders plot arrest and Judas arranges betrayal, a woman at Bethany pours costly perfume on Jesus; he interprets her act as preparation for burial and promises her memory wherever the good news is proclaimed. During Passover Jesus identifies betrayal, gives bread and cup as his body and covenant blood, and predicts the disciples' scattering. In Gethsemane he prays for the cup to pass yet submits to the Father's will while disciples sleep. Arrest, abandonment, competing testimony, a climactic Son of Man claim, abuse, and Peter's three denials carry the chapter to bitter weeping.
whyItMatters: Matthew surrounds Jesus's self-gift with failures of perception and loyalty. The unnamed woman understands death better than the Twelve; a shared table contains betrayal; prayer holds honest desire and obedience together; violence is refused; Scripture is fulfilled without making betrayers innocent; and Peter's collapse ends in grief rather than self-justification.

keyVerses.text: for this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.
keyVerses.why: The cup interprets the death through covenant, sacrificial pouring, the many, and release from sins.

keyVerses.text: He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.”
keyVerses.why: Submission is not absence of dread; Jesus voices his will honestly and entrusts it to the Father.

keyVerses.text: But all this has happened that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled.
keyVerses.why: Scriptural pattern and human failure converge without turning flight into faithful obedience.

questions.question: Why defend perfume instead of giving its value to the poor?
questions.answer: Jesus does not reject care for the poor; ‘you always have the poor with you’ echoes Deuteronomy 15, which commands an open hand because poverty remains. He recognizes a time-specific burial act that disciples dismiss. Their concern may sound righteous, but Matthew places it beside Judas's pricing of Jesus and the woman's costly recognition.

questions.question: Why keep the woman unnamed while promising her memory?
questions.answer: Matthew does not explain the anonymity. The effect is striking: male disciples argue and abandon, while an unnamed woman performs the act Jesus says will be told ‘in memory of her.’ Readers should resist filling the gap by automatically merging every Gospel anointing into one person; the traditions differ in setting, timing, and names.

questions.question: What does Judas's ‘thirty pieces of silver’ signal?
questions.answer: The amount evokes Zechariah 11's contemptuous valuation of a rejected shepherd and later shapes Matthew's fulfillment citation. Silver coin type is not specified here. The narrative contrast is moral as well as scriptural: lavish perfume honors Jesus while a disciple asks what he can get for handing him over.

questions.question: What do ‘this is my body’ and ‘this is my blood’ mean?
questions.answer: The meal interprets Jesus's approaching death through Passover, covenant, shared bread, and poured wine. Christian traditions differ over sacramental presence — transformation, real presence, spiritual participation, memorial, and combinations — because the terse ‘is’ does not provide a later philosophical explanation. All agree the act commands repeated communal remembrance and participation.

questions.question: Why ‘for many’ rather than ‘for all’?
questions.answer: The wording echoes Isaiah's servant who bears the sins of ‘many,’ where many is a great multitude and not necessarily a contrast excluding everyone else. Matthew's phrase emphasizes representative self-gift. It should be read with the Gospel's all-nations horizon rather than turned into arithmetic about whom Jesus intends to save.

questions.question: What is the ‘cup’ in Gethsemane?
questions.answer: Scripture uses a cup for an allotted fate and especially divine judgment. Jesus has offered disciples a covenant cup and now faces the suffering cup personally. Asking that it pass shows real dread, while ‘your will be done’ echoes the prayer of chapter 6 and makes obedience neither automatic nor emotionally numb.

questions.question: Does ‘the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak’ condemn bodies?
questions.answer: Sarx, flesh, here names vulnerable human capacity, not the body as evil substance. The disciples genuinely intend loyalty but cannot remain awake under grief and fear. Jesus commands watchful prayer because sincere intention alone does not overcome embodied weakness.

questions.question: Does fulfillment remove responsibility from Judas, leaders, or fleeing disciples?
questions.answer: No. Matthew can say the Son of Man goes ‘as written’ and still pronounce woe on the betrayer; Jesus can say Scripture is fulfilled while calling the arresting method wrong and the flight a failure. Divine purpose works through accountable human actions without relabeling betrayal as obedience.
